issues.legal_issue: A will cannot support a grant of letters of administration when the propounder fails to prove due execution and testamentary capacity or to dispel material suspicious circumstances with cogent evidence.
material_facts: The will was said to have been made shortly before the testator died, after he had suffered a paralytic stroke and been bedridden for months; the will itself described him as sick and getting weak.
No evidence from the doctor who treated the testator was produced to establish his mental and physical capacity when the will was made.

The attesting witness testified that the testator was paralysed and unable to write, and that the testator’s son, who was the sole beneficiary, did not know of the will during the eleven years he lived after its alleged execution.
The signature on the will appeared dissimilar to signatures in other documents, and the will’s text and signature did not appear to match.
The will was not produced for about fifteen years, until after the testator’s daughters sued for partition; the propounder gave no satisfactory explanation for its custody and delayed production.
The scribe was not identified or examined, the will did not state its date, and no evidence showed who had been instructed to prepare it.
The propounder and attesting witness gave discrepant accounts about whether she was present when the will was executed; other evidence supported the claim that the testator was gravely ill.
issues.conclusion: The propounders failed to prove the will in accordance with law or remove the suspicious circumstances surrounding its execution. The will was not validly proved, letters of administration could not be granted on its basis, and the trial court was right to dismiss the suit.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 59 and 63 of the Indian Succession Act, 1925, a testator must have testamentary capacity and the will must be signed and attested as prescribed; Sections 67 and 68 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, govern proof of signature and attested documents. The propounder must prove due execution and a sound and disposing state of mind, and must dispel legitimate suspicious circumstances with cogent, satisfactory evidence. The court must assess suspicious circumstances cumulatively and satisfy its conscience. The Court relied on H. Venkatachala Iyengar v. B.N. Thimmajamma, Jaswant Kaur v. Amrit Kaur, Bharpur Singh v. Shamsher Singh, Naranjan Umeshchandra Joshi v. Mrudula Jyoti Rao, B. Venkatamuni v. C.J. Ayodhya Ram Singh, Anil Kak v. Sharada Raje, and Leela Rajagopal v. Kamala Menon Cocharan.

rule.if: testamentary_grant_proceeding and will_challenged and (testator_seriously_ill_near_execution or signature_dissimilar or beneficiary_unaware_of_will or will_produced_after_long_delay or execution_accounts_conflict) and suspicious_circumstances_not_dispelled

predicates.testamentary_grant_proceeding: A person seeks a grant of probate or letters of administration on the basis of a will.
predicates.will_challenged: An opposing party disputes the will’s genuineness or due execution.
predicates.testator_seriously_ill_near_execution: Evidence indicates that the testator was seriously ill or physically or mentally impaired around the time the will was allegedly made.
predicates.signature_dissimilar: The signature on the disputed will appears materially different from the testator’s signatures on other documents.
predicates.beneficiary_unaware_of_will: A person who would substantially benefit from the will did not know of it during the testator’s lifetime.
predicates.will_produced_after_long_delay: The will was not produced until a substantial period after the testator’s death or after a dispute over the estate arose.
predicates.execution_accounts_conflict: Witnesses give materially inconsistent accounts of the circumstances in which the will was executed.
predicates.suspicious_circumstances_not_dispelled: The propounder does not provide cogent and satisfactory evidence that resolves the material doubts about the will’s execution or genuineness.

issues.definition: When a will is challenged in a proceeding for a testamentary grant and material suspicious circumstances remain unexplained, the will is not proved and cannot support letters of administration.

issues.legal_issue: A first appellate court that reverses a trial court must consciously reconsider the evidence and issues and give reasons for its contrary findings.
material_facts: The trial court considered the oral and documentary evidence and dismissed the suit after finding that the will’s execution remained suspicious and unproved.
The first appellate court reversed the trial court and decreed the suit in a short judgment that did not meaningfully reappraise the evidence or explain why the trial court’s findings were wrong.
The first appellate court did not give reasoned findings on the factual and legal issues pressed by the parties.
issues.conclusion: The first appellate court’s judgment was legally infirm because it reversed the trial court without adequate reasoning or reappreciation of the evidence. The Supreme Court set it aside and restored the trial court’s dismissal.
issues.legal_principle: Order XLI Rule 31 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, requires an appellate judgment to state the points for determination, the decision on them, the reasons, and the relief where a decree is reversed or varied. A first appeal is a valuable right and is open on fact and law; a court reversing factual findings must give its own cogent reasons after considering the evidence and the parties’ contentions. The Court relied on Santosh Hazari v. Purushottam Tiwari, B.V. Nagesh v. H.V. Sreenivasa Murthy, Vinod Kumar v. Gangadhar, and Madhukar v. Sangram.

rule.if: first_appeal_proceeding and reverses_trial_decision and (does_not_reappraise_evidence or does_not_give_reasons_on_issues)

predicates.first_appeal_proceeding: The proceeding is a first appeal from a trial court’s decision.
predicates.reverses_trial_decision: The appellate court changes or sets aside the trial court’s decision.
predicates.does_not_reappraise_evidence: The appellate court does not conscientiously reconsider the evidence relevant to the issues on appeal.
predicates.does_not_give_reasons_on_issues: The appellate court does not explain its findings on the issues and contentions that support its contrary decision.

issues.definition: When a first appellate court reverses a trial decision without reappraising the evidence or giving reasons on the issues, its reversal is unsustainable.
